'''''Hypoxis hirsuta''''', commonly known as '''common goldstar''',<ref>{{Cite PLANTS |symbol=HYHI2 |taxon=Hypoxis hirsuta}}</ref> '''common star-grass''',<ref>{{cite web |title=Hypoxis hirsuta (common star-grass): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/hypoxis/hirsuta/ |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref> '''eastern yellow stargrass''',<ref name="natureserve">{{cite web |title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.127933/Hypoxis_hirsuta |website=explorer.natureserve.org}}</ref> '''yellow star grass''',<ref name="IL">{{cite web |title=Yellow Star Grass (Hypoxis hirsuta) |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/prairie/plantx/yl_stargrassx.htm |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref> or '''yellow star flower''',<ref>{{cite web |title=Hypoxis hirsuta |url=https://plantfinder.nativeplanttrust.org/plant/Hypoxis-hirsuta |website=Native Plant Trust}}</ref> is a [[perennial]] [[ornamental plant]] in the family [[Hypoxidaceae]]. Sometimes this plant is placed in the family [[Amaryllidaceae]] or the family [[Liliaceae]]. The species is native to the [[United States]], [[Canada]], and northeastern [[Mexico]].<ref name="POW">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=279047 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>{{cite book | author=Blanchan, Neltje | author-link=Neltje Blanchan | title=[[Wild Flowers Worth Knowing]] | year=2005 | publisher=[[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]]}}</ref><ref>Espejo Serena, A. & López-Ferrari, A.R. (1996). Las Monocotiledóneas Mexicanas una Sinopsis Florística 1(6): 1-116. Consejo Nacional de la Flora de México, México D.F.</ref><ref name="bonap">[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Hypoxis%20hirsuta.png Biota of North America Program 2013 county distribution map]</ref>

==Description==
''H. hirsuta'' has grass-like, [[basal leaves]] that are up to {{convert |12|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on|}} long and one or more shorter stems, growing up from the rosette of leaves to {{convert |8|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on|}} long. The leaves have smooth margins and are elliptical in shape. Both the leaves and the stem have scattered white hairs.<ref name="IL"/>

Flowers appear April to May at the end of each stem in a group, or [[umbel]], of 2 to 6, occasionally only 1. The flowers are {{convert |5-13|mm|in|1|abbr=on|}} long, with 3 yellow [[petals]] and 3 yellow [[sepals]] spreading outwards. The flowers will open in the morning but typically wilt in the hot afternoon sun. When not flowering, the plant can resemble [[grass]], but it is not a grass.<ref name="MP">{{cite web |title=Hypoxis hirsuta page |url=http://www.missouriplants.com/Hypoxis_hirsuta_page.html |website=www.missouriplants.com}}</ref> 

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Hypoxis'' is from the Greek words hypo and oxys, meaning "sharp below", referring to how the seedpods have a tapered base. The specific epithet ''hirsuta'' is Latin for "hairy".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Denison |first1=Edgar |title=Missouri Wildflowers |date=2017 |publisher=Conservation Commission of the State of Missouri |isbn=978-1-887247-59-7 |pages=127 |edition=Sixth}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''H. hirsuta'' is native in the United States from New Mexico to the west, Texas to the south, the Canadian border to the north, and Maine to the east. In Canada, it is native in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Ontario. It is also native in northeastern Mexico, south to Tamualipas.<ref name="POW"/> The plant grows in moist to slightly dry habitats such as prairies, savannas, open woodlands, fens, glades, abandoned fields, and lawns.<ref name="IL"/>

==Ecology==
The flowers attract small bees that feed on its pollen.
